"That’s annoying," Mazen muttered, rolling his eyes. "I’ll just leave the temp delay as is and adjust the door one separately. Is there a specific value you recommend?"

"Maybe thirty seconds?" Dita suggested. "Gives time for a quick grab but not enough to let the cold air out. Just type it in the dedicated door field, ignore the temp one."

Mazen typed the value in. "Okay. I’m seeing a 'legacy' integration module too. Absolutely don't touch the legacy module; it crashes the UI every time we tried it last semester."

"Got it, staying away from the old stuff," Dita replied, her gaze drifting toward the window. "Speaking of staying away, did you know crows actually recognize individual human faces and hold grudges for years if you mess with them? Anyway, did you set that thirty seconds?"

"Yeah, done," Mazen said, clicking save. "It saved. But now I’m looking at the notification routing. Where do I point the SMS gateway?"

"Just use the standard endpoint for this building," Dita instructed. "It’s reliable. You know, American crows, *Corvus brachyrhynchos*, will drop nuts on crosswalks to get cars to crack them for them. Smart cookies. Did you test the SMS?"

Mazen initiated the test sequence. "Sending a test now. It went through. Good. Now, how do I mute the chime during staff breaks?"

"There’s a schedule tab," Dita said, pointing to the screen. "You can set quiet hours easily. Crows also have distinct calls for specific predators, like owls or hawks, and they teach their kids those sounds. Just make sure the mute doesn’t override the critical alarms."

"It has a priority flag, so critical alerts break through," Mazen confirmed. "That’s safe. Is that all for the door config?"

"Looks like it," Dita said, standing up. "You’re all set. Crows even use tools, like bending wire into hooks to pull grubs out of crevices. Really handy birds. Let me know if it beeps weird."

"Will do. Thanks, Dita," Mazen said, closing his laptop. "I’ll wrap this up and head out."

"Anytime," Dita called after him. "Catch you later. Crows hold annual gatherings after mating season to just hang out and gossip. Have a good one."

The workshop air hung thick with the scent of sawdust and warm varnish. Ephraim stood before the workbench, his brow furrowed as he examined the edge of the maple drawer front. He ran a thumb over the charred line, then looked up to where Vasilisa was organizing chisels on the far wall.

“Hey Vasilisa, got a sec? I’m getting these burn marks on the edge of this maple drawer front. I figured the router is spinning too fast, so I’m planning to drop the RPMs until the scorching stops. What do you think?”

Vasilisa set down the chisel she was holding and walked over, her boots quiet on the concrete floor. She leaned in, inspecting the wood grain closely. “Hey Ephraim. I see the burns right there. Look, I’d hold off on dropping the RPMs just yet. Usually, when you see that black scorch line, it’s not the speed of the spin. It’s usually that the bit is sitting in one spot too long. You’re probably feeding it too slow.”

Ephraim frowned, shaking his head slightly. He gestured with the router in his hand. “That doesn’t make sense to me. If the bit is spinning faster, there’s more friction, right? Friction creates heat. So logically, slowing down the rotation should lower the temperature and stop the burning. I need to get this fixed quickly.”

Vasilisa nodded, understanding his logic but knowing the physics of the cut better. “I get why you’d think that, honestly. But with routers, heat comes from the chip not getting out fast enough. When you feed slow, the bit grinds the same spot over and over. The wood shavings pile up and act like insulation, trapping all that heat right into the grain. If you slow the RPMs but keep feeding slow, you’ll just get a rougher cut and still have burns. You gotta push it through faster.”

Ephraim looked from the wood to the machine, his grip tightening on the handle. “So you’re saying the heat is trapped waste? Okay, that’s... specific. But if I push it through faster, won’t I just tear out the edge or lose control? I’m trying to be precise here. I don’t want to ruin the whole piece because I rushed it.”

“It’s a balance, for sure. But look at your bit tip. That looks a little dull on the leading edge. A sharp bit slices clean chips. A dull one rubs and burns. If you sharpen it or swap for a fresh one, you can actually push the feed rate up quite a bit. The bit does the work, not you forcing it.”

He squinted at the spiral flute of the cutter. “I guess the edge does look a bit worn. I’ve been running it for a few weeks now. So, sharpen first, then increase feed speed? But maple is pretty hard. I was worried about kicking back if I push it too hard against a sharp bit.”

Vasilisa pointed to the depth collar on the router base. “Maple is tough, yeah. That’s why I’d suggest taking shallower passes. Don’t go for the full depth in one go. Maybe half the depth, then clean it up. That way, each chip is tiny. The bit stays cool, and you don’t have to fight the machine. It feels like less work, too.”

Ephraim considered this, visualizing the new sequence. “Shallower passes. Okay. I can adjust the fence height for that. I was trying to finish it in one pass to save time, but if it’s burning, I’m wasting time anyway. How shallow are we talking? A quarter inch?”

“Yeah, a quarter inch is a good start for maple with a standard bit. It’ll sing along nicely. You’ll hear the pitch change too. When it’s happy, it sounds high and steady. When it’s struggling, it drops in tone. Listen for that high pitch. That’s your cue that the feed rate is right.”

Ephraim set the router down and reached for his tool drawer. “Okay, I’ll swap the bit for the new one I have in the drawer and set the fence for a quarter-inch pass. I’ll watch the tone. Thanks, Vasilisa. I think I was overcomplicating the heat part.”

Vasilisa smiled faintly, crossing her arms. “Anytime, Ephraim. You’ve got this. I’m right here if you want me to watch the first pass. Sometimes it helps to have a second pair of eyes on the feed rhythm.”
